ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Roo has a very unusual chessboard in which only the squares lying on the two diagonals are shaded. If the chessboard has side length 2003 squares, what is its total white area?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a schematic diagram of a square grid chessboard with an odd side length; gray shaded squares appear only on the two main diagonals; the two diagonals intersect at the same square in the center of the chessboard, so the center square belongs to both diagonals at the same time. Reasoning: The problem requires a chessboard with side length of 2003 squares. The total square area is 2003^2. Each diagonal has 2003 shaded squares, and the two diagonals together are first counted as 2003+2003, but the center square is counted repeatedly once, so the number of shaded squares is 2003+2003-1=4005. The white area equals the total area minus the shaded area: 2003^2-4005=2003^2-(2·2003-1)=(2003-1)^2=2002^2.

method.method_draft: Use a direct shaded-count complement. From the image, identify that the shaded squares form the two main diagonals of an odd-sized square grid, and the center square belongs to both diagonals. From the text, take the actual side length as 2003 squares and that all non-diagonal squares are white. Count shaded squares as 2003 on one diagonal plus 2003 on the other diagonal minus 1 for the shared center square, giving 4005 shaded squares. The total area is 2003^2 unit squares, so the white area is 2003^2 - 4005 = 2003^2 - (2·2003 - 1) = (2003 - 1)^2 = 2002^2.

From the image, observe that in each row of an odd-sized board, the two diagonals usually occupy two different squares, except in the middle row where they meet in one center square. From the text, set n = 2003. There are 2002 non-middle rows, each with 2003 - 2 = 2001 white squares, and 1 middle row with 2003 - 1 = 2002 white squares. Thus the total white area is 2002·2001 + 2002 = 2002(2001 + 1) = 2002^2.
